readingInstruction: Read Matthew 12:1-13:23. Jesus is Lord of the Sabbath, the Pharisees accuse him of working by Satan’s power, and he tells the first parables. Pay close attention to the parable of the sower and Jesus’ explanation.
settingTheScene: Opposition has been building, and in chapter 12 it becomes open conflict. The Pharisees object to Jesus’ disciples picking grain on the Sabbath and to his healing on the Sabbath. They then accuse him of casting out demons by Beelzebul. Jesus responds with arguments from Scripture and warnings. In chapter 13, he begins teaching in parables, stories that reveal the kingdom to those with ears to hear and conceal it from those who harden their hearts.
observation: “For the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath” (12:8).
“Behold, my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved with whom my soul is well pleased” (12:18).
“If I cast out demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you” (12:28).
“Whoever is not with me is against me” (12:30).
“For something greater than Solomon is here” (12:42).
“And he told them many things in parables, saying, A sower went out to sow” (13:3).
“As for what was sown on good soil, this is the one who hears the word and understands it. He indeed bears fruit” (13:23).
interpretation:
The Sabbath conflicts reveal a clash between two ways of reading God’s law. The Pharisees saw rules to protect. Jesus saw mercy to practice. He cites David, who ate the consecrated bread when hungry, and the priests who work in the temple on the Sabbath. Then he says, “Something greater than the temple is here,” and that the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath. This is a startling claim: he is the one who gave the Sabbath and the one to whom the Sabbath points.

Matthew quotes Isaiah’s servant song, showing a gentle servant who will not break a bruised reed. Then when Jesus casts out a demon, the Pharisees say he does it by the prince of demons. Jesus answers: a kingdom divided against itself cannot stand. If he casts out demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom has arrived. The unforgivable sin, blasphemy against the Spirit, is attributing the Spirit’s work to Satan, persistently and with a hardened heart. People who seek forgiveness have not committed it.

The parable of the sower begins chapter 13. A farmer scatters seed on four kinds of soil: the path, rocky ground, thorns, and good soil. The seed is the same. The difference is in the hearers. Some do not understand and the evil one snatches the word. Some receive it with joy but have no root. Some are choked by worries and wealth. And some hear, understand, and bear fruit. Jesus explains that parables reveal truth to those who are open and conceal it from those who are not.

The point is for you to ask which soil you are. The remedy for a hard heart is not to try harder but to ask the Sower to work on the soil.
connection: Exodus 20:8-11 gives the Sabbath command. Hosea 6:6 is quoted in 12:7. Isaiah 42:1-4 is quoted in 12:18-21. Mark 3:28-30 gives a parallel to the warning about the Spirit. Isaiah 6:9-10 is quoted in 13:14-15 about hardened hearts. Hebrews 4:1-11 teaches Sabbath rest fulfilled in Christ. Colossians 2:16-17 says the Sabbath was a shadow of what was to come. James 1:21 says to receive with meekness the implanted word.
application:
Honestly ask which soil describes you right now. If the thorns of worry or wealth are choking the word, name them.

Remember that Jesus is Lord of the Sabbath. Receive rest as a gift from him, not a rule to earn.

Pray for someone close to you who seems hard or unresponsive to the gospel.
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus for being Lord of the Sabbath.
Ask him to break up hard ground in your heart.
Ask him to help you bear fruit.
